Research on whether children learn language skills from television yields mixed and contested results. [d1] High-credibility sources indicate that well-designed educational programs—such as Sesame Street and Sesame Workshop apps—can improve cognitive, literacy, and social outcomes for children aged 3 to 5 [d2], and that educational programs may be beneficial for child language development, though quality varies considerably [d7]. However, other research presents a more skeptical view: a University of California study found that toddlers who watched the Baby Einstein DVD showed no greater language development than those who did not [d11], and a study of 275 young children found that TV viewing had no positive or negative effect on language development, with back-and-forth conversation being the most important predictor of future language skills [d12]. A peer-reviewed meta-analysis in JAMA Pediatrics further notes that screen time can displace opportunities to practice language and other developmental milestones, and that while educational programs show some promise, caution is needed due to variability in quality [d7]; the American Academy of Pediatrics similarly warns that active engagement with media may have some benefits but that real-time social interactions remain superior to digital media for learning [d10]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that television can be a helpful supplementary tool for language learning when programs are high-quality, co-viewing involves adult interaction, and children are not excessive viewers [d1][d2][d4], but that excessive screen time may negatively impact language development and that social interaction remains the most powerful driver of language acquisition [d6][d10][d12].
[[END-OF-ANSWER]]
